questions.question: When replying with a failed result, what does the is_error=true flag guard against?
options: The model resending the same doomed request unchanged
Replying an empty result or faking success, leaving the model to keep reasoning without knowing it failed
The client's retry loop running forever
questions.explanation: See the "is_error: let the model know it failed" section: is_error=true guards against two kinds of well-meant harm — replying an empty result and faking success — and only when the model plainly knows the request failed does self-correction have a chance.

questions.question: When a call hits a 429 rate limit, what does the lesson prescribe?
options: Reply the error and let the model itself wait a while before retrying
Keep retrying until success, since rate limits always pass
The client retries with exponential backoff (1s→2s→4s) under a retry cap
Abandon the task and report the error to the user
questions.explanation: See the "Backoff and caps: the client guardrail" section: rate limits and timeouts need waiting and retrying that only the client can do — exponential backoff paired with a retry cap (5 in this lesson's demo), because one never-recovering fault would otherwise drag the loop into infinite retries.

questions.question: Why reply with the verbatim error text from the validator or downstream service instead of a self-written "something went wrong"?
options: Because the API requires tool_result content to match the downstream response byte for byte
Because the verbatim text carries every clue the model needs — "expected YYYY-MM-DD, got 09/07" is already half the correct answer
Because the original text is usually shorter and saves context tokens
questions.explanation: See the "is_error: let the model know it failed" section: the original error message goes into content because the verbatim text carries every clue the model needs to fix its mistake — errors written for models should aim at actionability, not friendliness.
